Containers always provide stronger isolation than every VM
questions.explanation: Containers isolate processes using host-kernel facilities, while VMs commonly run separate guest kernels.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does preemptive scheduling allow?
options: A task must always run until exit
Every task controls the timer exclusively
The OS can suspend a running task to schedule another
questions.explanation: Preemption enables time sharing and priority responsiveness through OS-controlled task interruption.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is livelock?
options: A process waits only for one timer tick
Tasks keep reacting and changing state but make no useful progress
Tasks are permanently asleep without changing state
A disk block contains no data
questions.explanation: Unlike a static deadlock, livelocked participants remain active but fail to advance.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is an orphan process in Unix terminology?
options: A terminated child not yet reaped
A child whose parent has exited
questions.explanation: A living child can outlive its original parent and be reparented to an appropriate reaper.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does a page-table entry's dirty bit indicate?
options: The page has been modified since the relevant tracking point
The page has no virtual address
The page must always be discarded without writing
questions.explanation: Dirty tracking helps determine whether a modified page must be written back before reuse.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why can increasing a system's multiprogramming level eventually reduce throughput?
options: Combined working sets can trigger heavy paging
Every process automatically loses its files
questions.explanation: Excess demand for memory can cause thrashing, outweighing gains from overlapping CPU and I/O.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which protection principle limits the damage from a compromised service account?
questions.explanation: A minimally privileged account limits the resources an attacker can reach through that service.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is a buffer cache used for?
options: Keep recently used storage blocks in memory
questions.explanation: Caching blocks reduces repeated storage I/O and may combine writes, subject to consistency and durability policies.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Which IPC mechanism can communicate between processes on different hosts?
options: An inode number without a protocol
questions.explanation: Network sockets expose endpoints for inter-host communication using protocols such as TCP or UDP.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is priority inversion?
options: A high-priority task waits for a resource held by a lower-priority task while intermediate-priority work delays it
A high-priority task always runs first
questions.explanation: Priority inheritance can temporarily boost the lock holder to reduce this blocking pattern.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What does an atomic compare-and-swap operation do?
options: Update a value only if it equals an expected value, as one indivisible operation
questions.explanation: CAS supports lock-free algorithms by combining a comparison and conditional update atomically.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: Why are file permissions not equivalent to encryption?
options: Permissions control access through the OS; encryption protects data using keys
questions.explanation: Access control and encryption address different mechanisms and threat cases and can complement each other.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: For a fixed virtual address width, increasing page size changes the address split in what way?
options: Fewer offset bits and more page-number bits
Every page gets a separate CPU
More offset bits and fewer virtual page-number bits
The virtual address must double in length
questions.explanation: A larger power-of-two page needs more bits to select a byte within it, leaving fewer bits for the page number.

questions.subject: os
questions.question: What is reentrancy in code used by concurrent contexts?
options: The code must modify one unprotected global variable
The code runs only at boot
The code always has only one caller
The code can be safely entered again before an earlier invocation completes under its stated conditions
questions.explanation: Reentrant code avoids unsafe shared state or otherwise handles nested/concurrent invocations correctly.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does O(n) describe as an asymptotic upper bound?
options: An exact running time of n seconds
Growth bounded by a constant multiple of n for sufficiently large n
questions.explanation: Big-O describes growth up to constant factors beyond a threshold; it is not an exact elapsed time.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which notation expresses an asymptotically tight bound?
questions.explanation: Theta provides both asymptotic upper and lower bounds of the same order.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case time for linear search through n unsorted items?
questions.explanation: The target may be absent or last, requiring examination of all n items.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case time for binary search on a sorted random-access array?
questions.explanation: Each step discards roughly half the remaining interval.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Why does binary search not generally give logarithmic total time on an ordinary singly linked list?
options: Finding middle positions requires traversal rather than constant-time indexing
Linked lists cannot store sorted keys
Comparisons are forbidden on linked lists
questions.explanation: Although comparisons may be logarithmic, accessing successive middle elements is not constant time.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is amortized analysis used for?
options: Bounding average cost over a sequence of operations without requiring a probability distribution
questions.explanation: Amortized analysis spreads occasional expensive operations over a sequence, such as dynamic-array resizing.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: A dynamic array doubles capacity when full. What is the amortized append cost?
questions.explanation: Occasional O(n) copies are spread over enough cheap appends to give constant amortized cost.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Why does array indexing take constant time in the standard RAM model?
options: An element address is computed from base, index and element size
questions.explanation: Contiguous fixed-size elements allow direct address arithmetic.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case time to insert at the start of a packed array of n items when capacity is available?
questions.explanation: Existing items must shift one position to make space at the beginning.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is an advantage of contiguous arrays over linked lists during sequential scans?
options: No bounds checking can be used
No memory allocation is ever needed
questions.explanation: Nearby array elements tend to share cache lines, improving locality.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Given a pointer to the head, what is the cost of inserting a node at the front of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Only the new node's next pointer and the head pointer need to be adjusted.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What additional pointer does a doubly linked list normally store in each node?
options: A hash-table pointer for every key
A pointer to the previous node
A pointer to every other node
questions.explanation: A doubly linked node links both forward and backward, increasing storage but supporting reverse traversal.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Given only the head of a singly linked list, what is the worst-case cost of finding its last node?
questions.explanation: Without a maintained tail pointer, the list must be traversed to its end.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which technique detects a cycle in a linked list using constant auxiliary space?
questions.explanation: If a cycle exists, pointers moving at different speeds eventually meet inside it.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which data structure follows LIFO order?
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently inserted item first.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which data structure follows FIFO order?
questions.explanation: A queue removes items in insertion order, oldest first.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which data structure naturally supports matching nested parentheses?
questions.explanation: A stack tracks the most recent unmatched opening delimiter, preserving nesting order.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the main purpose of a circular queue in a fixed array?
options: Reuse freed positions without shifting all remaining items
questions.explanation: Wrapping indices around the array reuses positions released by dequeues.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What operations does a deque support?
options: Insertion and deletion at both ends
questions.explanation: A double-ended queue supports efficient updates at both front and rear.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure is naturally used by an iterative depth-first traversal?
questions.explanation: DFS explores a branch before backtracking, which matches stack behavior.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure is naturally used by breadth-first traversal?
questions.explanation: A FIFO queue processes vertices by discovery level.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is a leaf in a rooted tree?
questions.explanation: Leaf nodes have no children; the root is defined by having no parent.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: In a binary search tree with distinct keys, what order does inorder traversal produce?
questions.explanation: Inorder visits left subtree, root, then right subtree, matching the BST ordering invariant.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case search time in an unbalanced BST with n nodes?
questions.explanation: A skewed BST can form a chain of n nodes.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does an AVL tree require at each node?
options: Every node has exactly two children
Left and right subtree heights differ by at most one
Both subtrees contain equal numbers of keys
Every root key is the minimum
questions.explanation: The AVL balance condition bounds height and supports logarithmic search and updates.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which operation restores balance locally in self-balancing search trees?
questions.explanation: Rotations restructure parent-child links while preserving the inorder key ordering.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does a min-heap guarantee?
options: Every leaf is larger than every internal node
Every parent key is no greater than its children's keys
The left child is always smaller than the right
The entire array is globally sorted
It is a binary search tree
questions.explanation: The heap property is local between parents and children; it does not impose full sorted order.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the time to access the minimum of a nonempty binary min-heap?
questions.explanation: The minimum is stored at the root and can be read directly.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case time to remove the root of a binary heap?
questions.explanation: Replacing the root and restoring the heap property requires movement down at most the heap height.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the time complexity of bottom-up construction of a binary heap from n keys?
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near the leaves and require little sifting, making the total work linear.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure is particularly suitable for prefix searches on strings?
questions.explanation: A trie follows characters or symbols along paths and naturally supports prefix lookup.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure supports range-sum queries and point updates in O(log n)?
questions.explanation: A Fenwick tree stores structured partial sums for logarithmic updates and prefix sums; range sums use differences.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does a segment tree commonly support efficiently?
questions.explanation: Segment trees combine interval summaries and support logarithmic operations for suitable query/update types.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is a hash collision?
options: Different keys map to the same hash location or value
The same key is compared with itself
questions.explanation: Finite hash spaces can map distinct keys to the same result, requiring collision handling.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is separate chaining?
options: Storing colliding entries in a collection associated with each bucket
Using one bucket per possible key always
Storing all keys in a stack only
questions.explanation: Chaining keeps multiple entries in a bucket, often through a linked list or other local structure.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is open addressing?
options: Keeping entries in the table and probing for another slot after a collision
Keeping every collision in an external file
questions.explanation: Open-addressed tables locate alternative table slots using a probe sequence.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is primary clustering in linear probing?
options: Long runs of occupied adjacent slots attract more collisions
The table becomes a balanced tree
questions.explanation: Linear probing can build contiguous occupied clusters that lengthen probes.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the load factor for a hash table with n entries and m buckets?
questions.explanation: Load factor measures occupancy or average entries per bucket, depending on the collision scheme.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is expected hash-table lookup time with a suitable hash function and controlled load?
questions.explanation: Expected constant time depends on distribution and load assumptions; worst-case lookup can be linear.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Why is a tombstone useful when deleting from a linear-probing hash table?
options: It converts the table into a queue
It guarantees the table is sorted
It removes the need for rehashing forever
It preserves probe-chain reachability for later keys
questions.explanation: Simply marking a slot never-used can prematurely end a search for entries placed later in that probe chain.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly selects the smallest remaining item and places it next?
questions.explanation: Selection sort scans the unsorted portion for the next minimum.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which comparison sort is typically stable and has O(n log n) worst-case time?
options: Naive bubble sort without a pass limit
questions.explanation: Merge sort has logarithmic levels of linear merging and preserves ties when the merge chooses left equal keys first.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the worst-case time of ordinary quicksort with consistently poor pivots?
questions.explanation: Repeatedly splitting into sizes 0 and n−1 yields quadratic total partition work.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the average-case time of randomized quicksort?
questions.explanation: Random pivot choices give O(n log n) expected work, though the worst case remains quadratic.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which sort performs especially well on nearly sorted data and is stable in its usual implementation?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort does little shifting when data is nearly sorted and can preserve equal-key order.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does a stable sort preserve?
options: The memory address of every record
The original order of all records
The relative order of records with equal sort keys
questions.explanation: Stability matters when equal-key records already carry a meaningful earlier ordering.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which sort can run in O(n+k) for integer keys in a range of size k?
questions.explanation: Counting sort counts occurrences by key; its cost includes the input length and key-range size.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the lower bound for general comparison sorting in the worst case?
options: Omega(log n) as a tight bound
questions.explanation: A comparison decision tree must distinguish n! permutations, requiring logarithmic-of-factorial depth.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time and normally uses O(1) auxiliary array space?
options: Merge sort with an auxiliary array
questions.explanation: In-place heapsort builds a heap then repeatedly extracts the root; it is typically unstable.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Why does LSD radix sort require stable digit passes?
options: To replace every key with a hash
To guarantee one pass for all inputs
To preserve ordering established by less significant digits
questions.explanation: Stability ensures later passes do not destroy the ordering produced by earlier digit passes.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does a graph's adjacency matrix require for V vertices?
questions.explanation: The matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the space complexity of an adjacency-list graph representation?
questions.explanation: Vertex lists and edge entries together require linear space in vertices plus edges.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which algorithm finds shortest paths by number of edges in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS discovers vertices in nondecreasing distance from the source when all edges have equal weight.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which condition is needed for standard Dijkstra's algorithm to be generally correct?
options: The graph must be a tree
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy finalization relies on nonnegative edge weights.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which shortest-path algorithm handles negative edges and can detect a reachable negative cycle?
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes edges repeatedly and checks for further improvement after V−1 rounds.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does a topological ordering require?
options: A graph with only negative weights
A directed graph containing a cycle
questions.explanation: A DAG admits an ordering with each directed edge pointing forward; a directed cycle prevents such an ordering.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which algorithm constructs a minimum spanning tree by selecting edges in increasing weight order and avoiding cycles?
questions.explanation: Kruskal uses sorted edges and often a disjoint-set structure to detect cycles.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which algorithm grows a minimum spanning tree from a current tree using a cheapest crossing edge?
questions.explanation: Prim repeatedly adds the cheapest edge connecting the current tree to a new vertex.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure efficiently tracks connected components during Kruskal's algorithm?
questions.explanation: DSU supports finding representatives and merging components, enabling cycle checks.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does Floyd-Warshall compute?
options: A sorted list of edge labels
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall considers each vertex as an intermediate and uses O(V cubed) time.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: How can a graph be tested for bipartiteness?
options: Attempt a consistent two-coloring using BFS or DFS
Require every edge weight to be positive
Check that every vertex has even degree only
questions.explanation: A graph is bipartite exactly when its vertices can be two-colored with no same-color edge.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which property characterizes a tree among finite undirected graphs?
options: It has no edges regardless of vertex count
It contains a cycle through every vertex
questions.explanation: A tree is an undirected connected acyclic graph and has V−1 edges.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is a strongly connected directed graph?
options: Every vertex is reachable from every other vertex following edge directions
Every vertex has one outgoing edge
questions.explanation: Strong connectivity requires mutual directed reachability for all pairs.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS with adjacency lists?
questions.explanation: BFS visits each vertex and scans each adjacency entry a constant number of times.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What distinguishes dynamic programming from naive recursion for overlapping subproblems?
options: It only works on sorted arrays
questions.explanation: Memoization or tabulation avoids recomputing the same subproblems.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is optimal substructure?
options: An optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to relevant subproblems
Every greedy choice is automatically correct
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure is a key property used in many dynamic programming and greedy formulations.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the main difference between memoization and tabulation?
options: Memoization is typically top-down on demand; tabulation is typically bottom-up
questions.explanation: Both cache results, but their evaluation order and execution style differ.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: For the 0/1 knapsack problem, can an item be taken fractionally?
options: No; each item is taken whole or not taken
Only the lightest item can be taken
Every item must be taken twice
questions.explanation: The 0/1 formulation restricts each item to zero or one copy; fractional knapsack is a different problem.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which approach solves fractional knapsack optimally?
options: Always take the smallest value first
Greedily take highest value-to-weight ratios first
Use FIFO order regardless of ratio
Always take the heaviest item first
questions.explanation: With divisible items, the ratio-greedy strategy is optimal; it is not generally optimal for 0/1 knapsack.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is backtracking?
options: Explore choices and undo partial choices that cannot lead to a valid solution
Always choose one option without reconsidering
Store only final answers without search
questions.explanation: Backtracking explores a search tree and prunes invalid partial assignments.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is divide and conquer?
options: Store every input in one global variable
Split a problem into subproblems, solve them and combine their results
Try random answers until time expires
questions.explanation: Merge sort is a classic example: split, recursively sort, then merge.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which technique often finds a target-sum pair in a sorted array in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
questions.explanation: Comparing the end-pair sum lets one pointer advance without missing a valid pair.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which technique efficiently handles many fixed-length contiguous subarray calculations?
questions.explanation: A sliding window updates the aggregate as one element leaves and another enters.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: How do prefix sums answer static array range-sum queries after preprocessing?
options: Sort the queried range every time
questions.explanation: With a leading zero prefix, sum[l..r] equals prefix[r+1] minus prefix[l].

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the purpose of a base case in recursion?
options: Stop recursive expansion for a directly solvable case
questions.explanation: A correct base case and progress toward it ensure termination for valid inputs.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which resource can be exhausted by excessively deep ordinary recursion?
questions.explanation: Each active call typically consumes a stack frame unless an applicable optimization eliminates it.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does tail recursion mean?
options: The function sorts a linked-list tail only
The function calls two children always
The function contains no base case
The recursive call is the final operation whose result is directly returned
The recursive call occurs before all other work
questions.explanation: Tail calls have no pending work after the recursive return, though optimization depends on language and runtime.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does the KMP string-matching algorithm avoid through its prefix information?
options: Rechecking text characters after partial-match failures
questions.explanation: KMP reuses prefix/suffix structure to achieve O(n+m) matching time.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which string-search algorithm uses a rolling hash to compare candidate windows?
questions.explanation: Rabin-Karp updates a hash as the window moves and verifies candidate matches to handle collisions.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is a suffix array?
options: An array containing only the final character
An array of text suffix positions ordered lexicographically
questions.explanation: Suffix arrays index sorted suffixes and support text-search operations.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Can a standard Bloom filter produce a false positive?
options: Only when the set is empty
Only if it stores full keys
Yes; it may report possible membership for an absent item
questions.explanation: A Bloom filter is probabilistic: absent items may test positive, but inserted items do not test negative in its standard no-deletion form.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structures are commonly combined for O(1) expected LRU-cache lookup and updates?
options: Hash map and doubly linked list
Only a binary search on disk
Only a FIFO queue with no map
questions.explanation: The map locates entries; the doubly linked list maintains recency with constant-time node movement.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does path compression do in a disjoint-set forest?
options: Redirect visited nodes toward the representative during find
questions.explanation: Path compression flattens trees and, with rank or size heuristics, gives near-constant amortized operations.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which structure retrieves the highest-priority pending job efficiently?
options: Unsorted singly linked list with no scan
Ordinary FIFO queue regardless of priority
questions.explanation: A priority queue returns an item according to priority, often implemented with a heap.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which recurrence describes merge sort's main work on equal halves?
questions.explanation: Two recursive half-size sorts plus a linear merge produce Theta(n log n) time.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the auxiliary space of an iterative scan using only a fixed number of scalar variables?
questions.explanation: Auxiliary space excludes the input and remains constant when the working storage does not grow with input size.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the sum of degrees in an undirected graph with E edges and no unusual edge convention?
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes one incidence at each endpoint, giving total degree 2E; a loop contributes two.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is external sorting intended for?
options: Datasets too large to fit in main memory
questions.explanation: External sorting minimizes expensive storage I/O, commonly using sorted runs and multiway merging.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which traversal visits the root before its subtrees?
questions.explanation: Preorder visits root, then left and right subtrees in a binary tree.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which traversal visits children before the parent and is useful for deleting a tree?
questions.explanation: Postorder handles subtrees before their parent, useful when freeing child structures first.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Why does choosing the locally best option not prove a greedy algorithm is correct?
options: Sorting makes every local choice optimal
Every problem has one possible answer
Every greedy algorithm must enumerate all subsets
The problem also needs a valid greedy-choice argument linking local choices to a global optimum
questions.explanation: Greedy correctness needs proof, often an exchange argument, rather than intuition alone.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which grows faster asymptotically: n log n or n squared?
options: The answer depends only on CPU speed
questions.explanation: The ratio n squared divided by n log n is n/log n, which grows without bound.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the minimum number of edges in a connected undirected graph with V vertices?
questions.explanation: A spanning tree connects all V vertices with V−1 edges; fewer edges cannot connect them all.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What does rehashing typically involve when a table grows?
options: Keeping positions unchanged regardless of capacity
Deleting all occupied entries without copying
Recomputing positions and reinserting entries into a larger table
questions.explanation: Bucket positions often depend on capacity, so entries must be redistributed after growth.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Two stacks implement a queue by moving items only when the output stack is empty. What is amortized enqueue/dequeue time?
questions.explanation: Each item is pushed and popped a constant number of times across the operation sequence.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: In a full binary tree, how many children does each non-leaf node have?
questions.explanation: A full binary tree has either zero or two children at every node; it need not be perfect or balanced.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is a complete binary tree?
options: Every internal node has three children
A tree with sorted sibling keys only
Every leaf is at a different depth
Every node has exactly one child
All levels are full except possibly the last, which is filled left to right
questions.explanation: Completeness describes the shape used by array-based binary heaps.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which technique is especially appropriate for finding the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray in linear time?
questions.explanation: Kadane tracks the best sum ending at each position and the best sum overall.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: What is the time complexity of enumerating all subsets of an n-element set, ignoring output-copy cost?
questions.explanation: Each element can be included or excluded, yielding 2^n subsets.

questions.subject: dsa
questions.question: Which operation distinguishes a subsequence from a substring?
options: A subsequence may skip intervening characters while preserving order
A substring must contain the whole text
questions.explanation: Substrings are contiguous; subsequences preserve order but may omit positions.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command prints the current working directory?
questions.explanation: pwd reports the current directory; cd changes it.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command lists files, including names beginning with a dot?
questions.explanation: The -a option includes hidden dot entries in the listing.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does cd .. do?
options: Changes to the root directory always
questions.explanation: The .. entry refers to the current directory's parent.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command creates missing parent directories along a path?
questions.explanation: mkdir -p creates intermediate directories as necessary and tolerates existing directories.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What is an absolute pathname on Linux?
options: A path relative to the current directory
Any path beginning with a dot
questions.explanation: An absolute path starts at the root and does not depend on the current working directory.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command copies a file?
questions.explanation: cp makes a copy; mv moves or renames a file.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command renames old.txt to new.txt in the same directory?
questions.explanation: mv renames or moves its source; a same-directory rename changes the directory entry.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does touch existing.txt normally do when the file already exists?
questions.explanation: touch updates timestamps; if a named file does not exist, it normally creates an empty file.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command displays the last 20 lines of a file?
questions.explanation: tail -n selects the requested number of lines from the end.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command follows a growing log file?
questions.explanation: tail -f continues displaying appended data; tail -F adds name-following behavior useful for rotations on GNU systems.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command counts newline characters in a file?
questions.explanation: wc -l counts newline characters; a final unterminated line is an important edge case.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which GNU command searches under /var/log for regular files ending in .log?
questions.explanation: find traverses directories; quoting the pattern prevents the shell expanding it before find sees it.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command prints lines containing the literal string ERROR?
questions.explanation: grep selects matching lines; -F treats the pattern as a fixed string rather than a regular expression.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which grep option makes matching case-insensitive?
questions.explanation: grep -i ignores letter case when matching.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which grep option selects lines that do not match the pattern?
questions.explanation: grep -v inverts the match selection.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does sort -n do?
questions.explanation: Numeric sorting compares numbers rather than ordinary lexical order.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why is sort often used before uniq to remove duplicates throughout a file?
options: sort changes every line to lowercase
uniq works only on binary files
questions.explanation: Sorting makes identical lines adjacent so uniq can collapse them.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd print?
options: The first colon-separated field of each line
questions.explanation: The first field is the account name. Password hashes are normally stored in a separate protected shadow file.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does sed 's/error/warning/g' input.txt do by default?
options: Prints transformed text without modifying input.txt
questions.explanation: Without an in-place option or explicit write, sed writes transformed output to standard output.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: In awk, what does $1 usually refer to?
options: The last character of the filename
The first field of the current record
The exit code of the last shell command
questions.explanation: awk splits input records into fields; $0 is the whole record and $1 the first field.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does chmod 640 report.txt allow?
options: Owner all, group all, others none
Owner execute only, group execute only, others read
Owner read/write, group read, others no access
Owner read only, group write only, others execute
questions.explanation: Octal permissions use read=4, write=2 and execute=1: 6=rw, 4=r and 0=none.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does the execute permission on a directory primarily allow?
options: List every filename without read permission
Traverse/search the directory to access named entries
Execute every file without file permissions
questions.explanation: Directory execute means search/traversal. Directory read lists names; write controls directory-entry changes subject to other checks.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command changes file ownership?
questions.explanation: chown changes owner and optionally group; chmod changes permission bits.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does umask control?
options: The owner of every existing file
The encryption algorithm of the disk
Which permission bits are cleared from requested permissions for newly created objects
questions.explanation: A umask restricts initial permissions; it does not grant permissions that the creating program did not request.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does the sticky bit on a shared directory such as /tmp restrict?
options: How large every file must be
Who can remove or rename entries despite directory write permission
Who can read every file automatically
questions.explanation: The sticky bit generally limits deletion or renaming to the entry owner, directory owner or a privileged process.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why is chmod 777 usually inappropriate for a sensitive banking configuration file?
options: It encrypts the file too strongly
It grants every user read, write and execute permissions
It grants access only to root
questions.explanation: World-writable and world-readable sensitive files violate least privilege and can expose or alter secrets.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command prints the effective user's name?
questions.explanation: whoami reports the name associated with the effective user ID.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command shows a snapshot of processes in a common Linux format?
questions.explanation: ps displays process information; the BSD-style aux options are commonly used on Linux.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command provides an interactive process/resource display?
questions.explanation: top periodically updates process and system usage information.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which signal does kill PID send by default?
questions.explanation: SIGTERM requests termination and can be handled; SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why try SIGTERM before SIGKILL when stopping a service process manually?
options: It permits graceful cleanup if the program handles it
It always kills faster than SIGKILL
questions.explanation: Graceful termination can flush data and release resources; SIGKILL gives no cleanup opportunity.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does appending & to a shell command normally do?
options: Runs it asynchronously in the background
questions.explanation: The shell starts the command without waiting for completion before accepting the next command.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does jobs show in an interactive shell?
questions.explanation: Shell job control tracks foreground/background jobs belonging to that shell.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command resumes a stopped shell job in the foreground?
questions.explanation: fg makes a job the foreground job and resumes it if stopped; bg resumes it in the background.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What is nohup commonly used for?
options: Replace a service supervisor in every case
Run a command with hangup handling arranged so it can continue after logout
questions.explanation: nohup makes a command ignore SIGHUP and may redirect output; it is not a full service manager.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: For ordinary Linux nice values, what does a larger numeric nice value generally mean?
questions.explanation: A process that is more nice yields priority relative to lower nice values within the relevant scheduler class.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command reports filesystem free-space usage?
questions.explanation: df reports filesystem capacity and usage; -h formats sizes for humans.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command estimates space used by a directory tree?
questions.explanation: du sums allocated usage for the directory tree; -s summarizes and -h formats sizes.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command lists block devices on Linux?
questions.explanation: lsblk presents block devices and their relationships such as disks and partitions.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: On a systemd system, which command checks a service's status?
questions.explanation: systemctl status displays unit state and related information; the actual SSH unit name may be ssh or sshd by distribution.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What is the difference between systemctl start and systemctl enable?
options: enable always stops a running service
start activates now; enable configures activation through unit installation links, commonly at boot
questions.explanation: Starting and enabling are separate; enable --now combines enabling with immediate starting.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command displays journal entries for a systemd unit?
questions.explanation: journalctl queries the systemd journal; -u filters by unit.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which modern Linux command displays interface addresses?
questions.explanation: ip addr show displays configured IPv4/IPv6 addresses on interfaces.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command shows the IP routing table?
questions.explanation: ip route show displays routes, including a default route if configured.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which command commonly lists listening TCP sockets on Linux?
questions.explanation: ss inspects sockets; -l lists listeners, -t selects TCP and -n avoids name resolution.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which utility queries DNS records directly?
questions.explanation: dig queries DNS servers and displays response records and diagnostic information.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which line is a common Bash shebang?
questions.explanation: A shebang identifies the interpreter used when the executable script is launched by the system.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which is a valid Bash variable assignment?
questions.explanation: Shell assignment uses name=value with no spaces around the equals sign.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why should "$file" usually be quoted when passing a filename variable?
options: To prevent word splitting and pathname expansion of its value
To remove all spaces from the filename
questions.explanation: Double quotes preserve the expanded value as one argument while still allowing variable expansion.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: How do single quotes differ from double quotes in Bash?
options: Double quotes disable all variable expansion
Single quotes suppress variable and command substitution
questions.explanation: Single-quoted text is literal; double-quoted text still permits selected expansions such as $variable.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does $? expand to in Bash?
options: The exit status of the most recent foreground pipeline
questions.explanation: An exit status of zero conventionally means success; nonzero values indicate other outcomes.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does $# expand to in a shell script?
questions.explanation: $# counts positional arguments, excluding the script name $0.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why is "$@" commonly used to forward script arguments?
options: It prints only the last argument
It preserves each positional argument as a separate word
It merges all arguments without separators
It includes the process ID automatically
questions.explanation: Quoted "$@" expands to one word per positional parameter, preserving boundaries.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which Bash syntax performs command substitution?
questions.explanation: $(...) captures standard output, with trailing newlines removed, for use in an expansion.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which Bash syntax performs arithmetic expansion?
questions.explanation: Double parentheses inside $((...)) evaluate an arithmetic expression.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does command > out.txt do?
options: Preserves existing contents and appends always
Redirects standard output, normally truncating the file
questions.explanation: The > operator redirects file descriptor 1 and truncates an existing file under normal settings.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does command >> out.txt do?
options: Deletes the file after the command
Appends standard output to the file
Overwrites the file from the beginning always
questions.explanation: The >> operator opens the destination for appending stdout.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does 2> errors.txt redirect?
options: All files opened by the command
questions.explanation: File descriptor 2 is standard error; 0 is input and 1 is output.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: In command >all.log 2>&1, where do stdout and stderr go?
options: Only stdout to all.log; stderr stays unchanged
questions.explanation: Redirections are applied left to right: stdout opens the file, then stderr duplicates that destination.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: In command 2>&1 >out.log, where does stderr go if stdout initially points at the terminal?
questions.explanation: stderr duplicates the old stdout before stdout is redirected to the file; order matters.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does a shell pipe connect by default?
options: One user's password to another user
The CPU to the disk controller
Every command's stderr to all files
One command's stdout to the next command's stdin
questions.explanation: The pipe operator connects standard output to standard input; stderr is separate unless redirected.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: When does cmd2 run in cmd1 && cmd2?
options: Only if both are background jobs
questions.explanation: The AND list runs the second command when the first returns zero.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: When does cmd2 run in cmd1 || cmd2?
options: Only when cmd1 is a shell builtin
When cmd1 returns a nonzero exit status
questions.explanation: The OR list runs the second command if the first fails according to its exit status.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: In [ -f "$path" ], what does -f test?
options: Whether the path resolves to a regular file
Whether the file is larger than 1 GB
Whether the path is a directory
questions.explanation: The -f test checks for a regular file; -d checks for a directory.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Which integer comparison operator means equal inside traditional [ ... ] tests?
questions.explanation: -eq compares integers. String and file tests have different operators.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: In a standard five-field crontab, what does 0 2 * * * specify?
options: Every day at 02:00 in cron's configured timezone
questions.explanation: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What does tar -czf backup.tar.gz reports/ do?
options: Encrypts the archive with a password
questions.explanation: -c creates, -z uses gzip and -f names the archive; compression is not encryption.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why use read -r when reading arbitrary text in a shell loop?
options: To avoid treating backslashes as escapes
To execute each line as code
questions.explanation: read -r preserves backslashes; IFS handling is a separate consideration for whitespace.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: Why should untrusted text not be passed to eval?
options: eval always converts text to numbers
It can be interpreted as shell code
questions.explanation: eval reparses its input as shell syntax, which can turn attacker-controlled data into commands.

questions.subject: linux
questions.question: What is the purpose of -- in a command such as rm -- "$file"?
options: End option parsing so a dash-leading filename is treated as an operand
questions.explanation: Many utilities accept -- to separate options from operands; quoting and option termination solve different problems.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For an ordinary IPv4 /24 LAN subnet, excluding network and broadcast addresses, how many usable host addresses exist?
questions.explanation: Host bits = 32−24 = 8. Usable hosts = 2^8−2 = 254. /31 and /32 special cases are not involved.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /24?
questions.explanation: A /24 mask has 24 leading one bits; its dotted form is 255.255.255.0.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.1.3.141/25?
questions.explanation: Apply the /25 mask to 10.1.3.141. The containing subnet is 10.1.3.128/25, beginning at 10.1.3.128.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.30.64/27?
questions.explanation: The /27 block contains 32 addresses: .64 through .95. Its last address, 192.168.30.95, is broadcast.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the last usable host address in the ordinary IPv4 subnet 172.16.2.128/26?
questions.explanation: The broadcast address is 172.16.2.191; the immediately preceding address 172.16.2.190 is the last usable host.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How many /25 subnets fit into a /24 IPv4 network?
questions.explanation: 1 additional prefix bits create 2^1 = 2 subnets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the longest IPv4 prefix that provides at least 25 usable host addresses in an ordinary LAN subnet?
questions.explanation: Need 2^h−2 ≥ 25. The smallest h is 5, giving 30 hosts and /27.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is the correctly compressed form of 2001:0db8:0001:0000:0000:0000:0000:00a0?
questions.explanation: Remove leading zeroes in hextets and compress the consecutive zero run once: 2001:db8:1::a0.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How many /64 IPv6 subnets fit inside a /48 allocation?
questions.explanation: There are 64−48 = 16 subnet bits, giving 2^16 = 65536 subnets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An IPv4 packet starts with TTL 32. What TTL remains after 3 routers each decrement it once, with no encapsulation?
questions.explanation: TTL decreases once at each forwarding router: 32−3 = 29.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Ignoring headers and other delays, how long does serializing 500 bytes onto a 10 Mbps link take?
questions.explanation: Time = bits/rate = 500×8 / 10,000,000 seconds = 0.4 ms.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A signal travels 100 km at 200,000 km/s. What is its one-way propagation delay?
questions.explanation: Delay = distance/speed = 100/200,000 seconds = 0.5 ms.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For a 10 Mbps link and 20 ms round-trip time, what is the bandwidth-delay product in bytes? Use decimal units.
questions.explanation: 10×1,000,000×0.020 bits ÷ 8 = 25000 bytes. This is the bandwidth multiplied by RTT.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A stop-and-wait sender takes 1 ms to transmit a data frame. Round-trip propagation is 2 ms; ACK transmission and processing are negligible. What is sender utilization?
questions.explanation: One cycle takes transmission plus round-trip propagation: 1+2 ms. Utilization = 1/(1+2)×100 = 33.33%.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A sender has a 16000-byte usable send window and sends 1000-byte payload segments. Ignoring other limits, how many full segments may be outstanding?
questions.explanation: Window divided by payload = 16000/1000 = 16 full segments.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A CRC generator polynomial has degree 3. How many CRC remainder bits are appended to a dataword?
questions.explanation: A generator of degree r uses r remainder/check bits. Here r = 3.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What bit must be appended to 1011001 to make the total number of 1 bits even?
questions.explanation: The data contains 4 one bits. Add 0 so the resulting count is even.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For single-bit-error-correcting Hamming coding of 4 data bits, what is the minimum parity-bit count r satisfying 2^r ≥ m+r+1?
questions.explanation: The smallest r satisfying 2^r ≥ 4+r+1 is 3: 2^3 = 8 ≥ 8.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For an ideal noiseless 2000 Hz channel using 2 signal levels, what is the Nyquist maximum bit rate in bits/s?
questions.explanation: Rate = 2B log2(M) = 2×2000×1 = 4000 bits/s.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram has 2000 bytes of payload and a 20-byte header. It crosses a link with MTU 1000; fragmentation is allowed, with no options. How many fragments are needed?
questions.explanation: Nonfinal fragment payload must be a multiple of 8: floor((1000−20)/8)×8 = 976 bytes. ceil(2000/976) = 3 fragments.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A TCP segment starts at sequence number 1000 and carries 200 data bytes, with no SYN or FIN. If all bytes through this segment arrive in order, which ACK number is expected?
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledges the next expected byte: 1000+200 = 1200.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is the conventional destination port for SSH?
questions.explanation: The conventional service port for SSH is 22; servers may be configured to use different ports.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Successful recoverable snapshots are taken every 5 minutes. If a failure occurs just before the next snapshot and no later logs exist, what is the worst-case lost-work interval in minutes, approximately?
questions.explanation: The latest recoverable point may be almost one snapshot interval old, so potential loss is approximately 5 minutes.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A recovery plan needs 10 minutes to restore, then 5 minutes to validate, then 2 minutes to switch traffic. With no overlap, what is total restoration time in minutes?
questions.explanation: Add the sequential stages: 10+5+2 = 17 minutes.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A service is observed for 10,000 minutes with 99% availability. How many minutes was it unavailable?
questions.explanation: Unavailable fraction = (100−99)/100. Multiply by 10,000 to obtain 100 minutes.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For an ordinary IPv4 /25 LAN subnet, excluding network and broadcast addresses, how many usable host addresses exist?
questions.explanation: Host bits = 32−25 = 7. Usable hosts = 2^7−2 = 126. /31 and /32 special cases are not involved.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal mask corresponds to /25?
questions.explanation: A /25 mask has 25 leading one bits; its dotted form is 255.255.255.128.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the network address of 10.2.3.144/26?
questions.explanation: Apply the /26 mask to 10.2.3.144. The containing subnet is 10.2.3.128/26, beginning at 10.2.3.128.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.31.64/27?
questions.explanation: The /27 block contains 32 addresses: .64 through .95. Its last address, 192.168.31.95, is broadcast.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the last usable host address in the ordinary IPv4 subnet 172.16.3.128/27?
questions.explanation: The broadcast address is 172.16.3.159; the immediately preceding address 172.16.3.158 is the last usable host.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How many /26 subnets fit into a /24 IPv4 network?
questions.explanation: 2 additional prefix bits create 2^2 = 4 subnets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What is the longest IPv4 prefix that provides at least 50 usable host addresses in an ordinary LAN subnet?
questions.explanation: Need 2^h−2 ≥ 50. The smallest h is 6, giving 62 hosts and /26.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is the correctly compressed form of 2001:0db8:0002:0000:0000:0000:0000:00a1?
questions.explanation: Remove leading zeroes in hextets and compress the consecutive zero run once: 2001:db8:2::a1.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: How many /64 IPv6 subnets fit inside a /52 allocation?
questions.explanation: There are 64−52 = 12 subnet bits, giving 2^12 = 4096 subnets.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An IPv4 packet starts with TTL 40. What TTL remains after 4 routers each decrement it once, with no encapsulation?
questions.explanation: TTL decreases once at each forwarding router: 40−4 = 36.

questions.question: A signal travels 200 km at 200,000 km/s. What is its one-way propagation delay?
questions.explanation: Delay = distance/speed = 200/200,000 seconds = 1 ms.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For a 20 Mbps link and 20 ms round-trip time, what is the bandwidth-delay product in bytes? Use decimal units.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A CRC generator polynomial has degree 4. How many CRC remainder bits are appended to a dataword?
questions.explanation: A generator of degree r uses r remainder/check bits. Here r = 4.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: What bit must be appended to 1110000 to make the total number of 1 bits even?

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For single-bit-error-correcting Hamming coding of 8 data bits, what is the minimum parity-bit count r satisfying 2^r ≥ m+r+1?
questions.explanation: The smallest r satisfying 2^r ≥ 8+r+1 is 4: 2^4 = 16 ≥ 13.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: For an ideal noiseless 2000 Hz channel using 4 signal levels, what is the Nyquist maximum bit rate in bits/s?
questions.explanation: Rate = 2B log2(M) = 2×2000×2 = 8000 bits/s.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram has 2500 bytes of payload and a 20-byte header. It crosses a link with MTU 1000; fragmentation is allowed, with no options. How many fragments are needed?

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A TCP segment starts at sequence number 2000 and carries 300 data bytes, with no SYN or FIN. If all bytes through this segment arrive in order, which ACK number is expected?
questions.explanation: TCP acknowledges the next expected byte: 2000+300 = 2300.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Which is the conventional destination port for SMTP server-to-server?
questions.explanation: The conventional service port for SMTP server-to-server is 25; servers may be configured to use different ports.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: Successful recoverable snapshots are taken every 10 minutes. If a failure occurs just before the next snapshot and no later logs exist, what is the worst-case lost-work interval in minutes, approximately?
questions.explanation: The latest recoverable point may be almost one snapshot interval old, so potential loss is approximately 10 minutes.

questions.subject: network
questions.question: A recovery plan needs 15 minutes to restore, then 6 minutes to validate, then 2 minutes to switch traffic. With no overlap, what is total restoration time in minutes?
